\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Smooth numbers and sieve yield}

A positive integer $v$ is \emph{$B$-smooth} if every prime factor of $v$ is at most $B$. Write
\[
\Psi_B(x) = \#\{v \in \ZZ : 1 \le v \le x,\ v \text{ is } B\text{-smooth}\},
\]
the \emph{smooth-counting function}; let $\pi(B)$ be the number of primes $\le B$ (the size of the \emph{factor base}) and $P_B = \prod_{p \le B} p$ its \emph{primorial}.

Smooth numbers are the computational substrate of subexponential integer factorization. A sieve generates candidate values, tests each for $B$-smoothness, retains the survivors, and assembles their factorization exponent vectors into a linear system over $\FF_2$; a nontrivial kernel vector yields a congruence of squares. The dominant cost parameter is the \emph{yield}: the proportion of candidates that survive.

Asymptotically the yield is governed by the \emph{smoothness parameter} $u = \log x/\log B$ via $\Psi_B(x) \sim x\,\rho(u)$, with $\rho$ the Dickman function. In the \emph{tight-$u$ regime} that real sieves inhabit, roughly $2 \le u \le 5$, the asymptotic is too coarse for per-instance prediction.

\subsection{The empirical residual}

A programme of experiments built regression models predicting per-instance yield. A strong baseline used candidate magnitude, the bound $B$, the derived $u$, and the \emph{squarefree hit indicators} $\one[p \mid v]$ for factor-base primes $p$. That baseline left a structured residual.

Two natural extensions failed: mid-prime fractions of the factor base contributed $+0.019$ out-of-sample $R^2$ with confidence interval spanning zero; quadratic-residue density contributed $+0.004$, likewise. A third succeeded decisively: \emph{prime-power hit indicators} $\one[p^2 \mid v]$ for $p \le 13$ added $+0.0892$ out-of-sample $R^2$ with confidence interval $[0.041, 0.125]$, over the full baseline.

This paper explains that gain structurally, by exact identities showing that the squarefree indicators and the higher prime-power indicators occupy provably disjoint informational layers, and that the higher layers reconstruct exactly the quantity the yield depends on.

\section{Definitions and conventions}

Throughout, $B, m, v, w, x, j, k$ are non-negative integers and $p, q$ are primes. Integer divisions are floor divisions.

\begin{definition}[Smoothness]
For $B, v \in \NN$, say $v$ is \emph{$B$-smooth}, written $\Sm_B(v)$, if every prime $p$ dividing $v$ satisfies $p \le B$. By convention $\Sm_B(1)$ holds vacuously; we always restrict to $v \ge 1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Closure properties]\label{lem:closure}
Smoothness passes to divisors and is multiplicative: if $d \mid n$, $n \ne 0$ and $\Sm_B(n)$, then $\Sm_B(d)$; and if $a, b \ne 0$ with $\Sm_B(a)$, $\Sm_B(b)$, then $\Sm_B(ab)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Any prime of $d$ is a prime of $n$. The prime support of $ab$ is the union of the supports of $a$ and $b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Counting functions]
\[
\Psi_B(x) = \#\{v : 1 \le v \le x,\ \Sm_B(v)\},
\qquad
\hit_B(m; x) = \#\{v : 1 \le v \le x,\ \Sm_B(v),\ m \mid v\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Budget]
$\Omega(v)$ is the number of prime factors of $v$ with multiplicity, so $\Omega(v) = \sum_p v_p(v)$ where $v_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation. We call $\Omega$ the \emph{discrete smoothness budget}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Feature vectors]
Let $\mathcal{P}_B$ be the set of primes $\le B$, so $|\mathcal{P}_B| = \pi(B)$. Define the \emph{squarefree hit vector} and \emph{prime-power hit vector}
\[
\sqf_B(v) = \{p \in \mathcal{P}_B : p \mid v\},
\qquad
\pw_B(v) = \{p \in \mathcal{P}_B : p^2 \mid v\}.
\]
The \emph{prime-power hit profile} of $v$ is the family $\big(\one[p^j \mid v]\big)_{p \in \mathcal{P}_B,\ j \ge 1}$; the squarefree vector is its $j = 1$ layer.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
For $B > 1$, $x \ge 1$, the smoothness parameter is $u_B(x) = \log x/\log B$.
\end{definition}

\section{The exact rescaling theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exact rescaling]\label{thm:rescale}
Let $m > 0$ with $\Sm_B(m)$. Then for all $x$,
\[
\hit_B(m; x) \;=\; \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/m \rfloor\big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
We exhibit mutually inverse maps. Forward: $v \mapsto v/m$. If $1 \le v \le x$, $\Sm_B(v)$ and $m \mid v$, then $v/m$ is an integer with $1 \le v/m \le \lfloor x/m\rfloor$, and $v/m \mid v$ gives $\Sm_B(v/m)$ by Lemma \ref{lem:closure}. Backward: $w \mapsto mw$. If $1 \le w \le \lfloor x/m\rfloor$ and $\Sm_B(w)$, then $mw \le x$ by the defining property of floor division, $\Sm_B(mw)$ by multiplicativity (using $\Sm_B(m)$), and $m \mid mw$. The maps are mutually inverse since $m \cdot (v/m) = v$ when $m \mid v$, and $(mw)/m = w$ as $m > 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Prime-square hit]\label{cor:psq}
For a prime $p \le B$ and all $x$, $\hit_B(p^2; x) = \Psi_B(\lfloor x/p^2\rfloor)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The only prime factor of $p^2$ is $p \le B$, so $\Sm_B(p^2)$; apply Theorem \ref{thm:rescale}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Joint hits compose multiplicatively]\label{cor:joint}
For distinct primes $p, q \le B$,
\[
\#\{v \le x : \Sm_B(v),\ p^2 \mid v,\ q^2 \mid v\} \;=\; \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/(p^2q^2)\rfloor\big).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$p^2$ and $q^2$ are coprime, so simultaneous divisibility is equivalent to divisibility by $p^2q^2$, a $B$-smooth modulus; apply Theorem \ref{thm:rescale}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Smoothness of the modulus is necessary]\label{rem:necessary}
Take $B = 5$, $m = 7$, $x = 100$. No $5$-smooth number is divisible by $7$, so $\hit_5(7;100) = 0$, while $\Psi_5(14) = |\{1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12\}| = 10$. The failure is total: the backward map $w \mapsto mw$ leaves the smooth pool.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}
For $m \ge 2$ and $x \ge 1$, $\hit_B(m;x) < \Psi_B(x)$, since $v=1$ is smooth but never hit. For $B \le B'$, $\hit_B(m;x) \le \hit_{B'}(m;x)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Graded valuation spectrum]\label{thm:graded}
For a prime $p \le B$ and $j \ge 0$,
\[
\#\{v \le x : \Sm_B(v),\ v_p(v) = j\} \;=\; \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/p^j\rfloor\big) - \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/p^{j+1}\rfloor\big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $S_k = \{v \le x : \Sm_B(v),\ p^k \mid v\}$. For $v \ne 0$, $p^k \mid v \iff k \le v_p(v)$, so $S_{j+1} \subseteq S_j$ and the exact-multiplicity stratum is $S_j \setminus S_{j+1}$. Each $p^k$ is $B$-smooth, so $|S_k| = \Psi_B(\lfloor x/p^k\rfloor)$ by Theorem \ref{thm:rescale}; cardinality of a difference of nested finite sets subtracts.
\end{proof}

\section{The budget shift and the tight-$u$ mechanism}

\begin{theorem}[Exact budget shift]\label{thm:shift}
Let $p > 0$, $v > 0$ with $p^2 \mid v$. Then for any base $B$,
\[
u_B(v) \;=\; u_B(v/p^2) + \frac{2\log p}{\log B}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $v = p^2 w$ with $w > 0$; then $v/p^2 = w$ exactly and $\log v = 2\log p + \log w$. Divide by $\log B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{budget toll} of a $p^2$-hit at bound $B$ is $\delta_B(p) = 2\log p/\log B$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Budget squeeze]\label{thm:squeeze}
Let $B > 1$, $p > 0$ and $p^2 \le x$. Then $u_B(\lfloor x/p^2\rfloor) \le u_B(x) - \delta_B(p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\lfloor x/p^2\rfloor \ge 1$ by hypothesis, and $\lfloor x/p^2\rfloor \le x/p^2$ as reals; monotonicity of $\log$ gives $\log\lfloor x/p^2\rfloor \le \log x - 2\log p$. Divide by $\log B > 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The hypothesis $p^2 \le x$ is required: if $x < p^2$ then $\lfloor x/p^2\rfloor = 0$ and the left-hand side degenerates. This is a genuine boundary condition, not an artefact.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Antitonicity of the toll]\label{thm:antitone}
For $1 < B \le B'$ and $p \ge 1$,
\[
\delta_{B'}(p) = \frac{2\log p}{\log B'} \;\le\; \frac{2\log p}{\log B} = \delta_B(p).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$0 < \log B \le \log B'$ by monotonicity of $\log$; the numerator $2 \log p$ is nonnegative; and $t \mapsto c/t$ is antitone on $t > 0$ for $c \ge 0$.
\end{proof}

The same arithmetic event consumes a larger share of the budget at a smaller factor-base bound: $\delta_{10^6}(2) \approx 0.100$ but $\delta_{13}(2) \approx 0.541$, and $\delta_{13}(13) = 2$. Because $\rho(u)$ decays super-exponentially, a half-unit shift in $u$ is a first-order effect at tight $u$ and negligible at large $B$. This is exactly the observed regime dependence.

\section{Completeness of the prime-power profile}

\begin{theorem}[Complete invariant]\label{thm:complete}
Let $v, w > 0$ be $B$-smooth, and suppose $p^j \mid v \iff p^j \mid w$ for every prime $p \le B$ and every $j \ge 1$. Then $v = w$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By unique factorization it suffices to prove $v_p(v) = v_p(w)$ for all primes $p$. If $p \le B$: from $p^{v_p(v)} \mid v$ we get $p^{v_p(v)} \mid w$, hence $v_p(v) \le v_p(w)$, and symmetrically. If $p > B$: smoothness forces both valuations to vanish. If $p$ is not prime, both vanish by convention.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict refinement]\label{thm:refine}
Let $p \le B$ be prime, $v \ne 0$, $p \mid v$, $p^2 \nmid v$. Then $\sqf_B(vp) = \sqf_B(v)$, while $p \in \pw_B(vp)$ and $p \notin \pw_B(v)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first claim is the $k=1$ case of Theorem \ref{thm:blind}. For the second, $v = pw$ gives $vp = p^2 w$. The third is the hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\section{The budget decomposition}

\begin{lemma}[Budget as a factor-base sum]\label{lem:bfb}
If $\Sm_B(v)$ then $\Omega(v) = \sum_{p \le B} v_p(v)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
In general $\Omega(v)$ is the sum of valuations over the prime support of $v$; smoothness puts that support inside $\mathcal{P}_B$, and the extra terms are zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A valuation counts hits]\label{lem:valcount}
Let $p$ be prime, $v \ne 0$, and $J \ge v_p(v)$. Then $v_p(v) = \#\{j \in [1,J] : p^j \mid v\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $v \ne 0$, $p^j \mid v \iff j \le v_p(v)$; the filtered set is $[1, v_p(v)]$, of cardinality $v_p(v)$.
\end{proof}

The window $J = \lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor$ always suffices for $v \le x$: for any prime $p$, $2^{v_p(v)} \le p^{v_p(v)} \le v \le x$, so $v_p(v) \le \log_2 x$.

\begin{theorem}[Budget decomposition, hit form]\label{thm:decomp}
For all $B, x$,
\[
\sum_{\substack{1 \le v \le x \\ \Sm_B(v)}} \Omega(v)
\;=\;
\sum_{p \le B}\ \sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor} \hit_B(p^j; x).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $v$ in the pool, Lemma \ref{lem:bfb} and Lemma \ref{lem:valcount} at $J = \lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor$ give
$\Omega(v) = \sum_{p\le B}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\one[p^j \mid v]$. Summing over $v$ and exchanging the finite orders of summation, the $(p,j)$ term becomes $\#\{v \le x : \Sm_B(v),\ p^j\mid v\} = \hit_B(p^j;x)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Budget decomposition, rescaled form]\label{thm:decomp2}
For all $B, x$,
\[
\sum_{\substack{1 \le v \le x \\ \Sm_B(v)}} \Omega(v)
\;=\;
\sum_{p \le B}\ \sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor} \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/p^j\rfloor\big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem \ref{thm:rescale} to each modulus $p^j$, which is $B$-smooth since $p \le B$.
\end{proof}

The total smoothness budget of the pool is thus a \emph{linear} functional --- indeed the plain sum --- of the prime-power hit counts. The prime-power features do not approximate the budget; they are the budget in a different basis. The squarefree features are exactly the layer $j = 1$, one slice of a stack $\lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor$ deep.

\section{What the squarefree layer cannot see}

\begin{theorem}[Blindness of the squarefree features]\label{thm:blind}
Let $p$ be prime with $p \mid v$, $v \ne 0$, and $k \ge 0$. Then
\[
\sqf_B(v \cdot p^k) = \sqf_B(v),
\qquad
\Omega(v \cdot p^k) = \Omega(v) + k.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The multiset of prime factors of $vp^k$ is that of $v$ together with $k$ copies of $p$, so lengths add. For a prime $q \le B$: if $q \mid vp^k$ then $q \mid v$ or $q = p$, and $p \mid v$ by hypothesis; the converse is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact impossibility]
The fibres of $v \mapsto \sqf_B(v)$ contain values of arbitrarily large budget. Hence no function $F$ satisfies $F(\sqf_B(v)) = \Omega(v)$ for all smooth $v$: budget information is absent from the squarefree layer, not merely attenuated.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Forced collisions]\label{thm:collide}
If $2^{\pi(B)} < \Psi_B(x)$, then there exist distinct $B$-smooth $v, w \in [1,x]$ with $\sqf_B(v) = \sqf_B(w)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\sqf_B$ maps the pool into the power set of $\mathcal{P}_B$, of cardinality $2^{\pi(B)}$; pigeonhole.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unconditional at $B=2$]
For every $x \ge 4$ there exist distinct $2$-smooth $v, w \in [1,x]$ with $\sqf_2(v) = \sqf_2(w)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\pi(2) = 1$ gives only $2$ possible vectors, while $\Psi_2(x) = \lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor + 1 \ge 3$ for $x \ge 4$ by Theorem \ref{thm:psi2}. Explicitly $v=2$, $w=4$ both have vector $\{2\}$.
\end{proof}

Contrast Theorem \ref{thm:complete}: the full profile never collides. Truncation to $j=1$ is exactly what destroys the invariant.

\section{Abundance}

\begin{theorem}[Abundance]\label{thm:abund}
If $P_B^{\,m} \le x$ then $\Psi_B(x) \ge (m+1)^{\pi(B)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Index candidates by exponent vectors $f : \mathcal{P}_B \to \{0,\dots,m\}$ and set $F(f) = \prod_{p \le B} p^{f(p)}$. Each $F(f)$ is positive, $B$-smooth, and $\le \prod_{p\le B}p^m = P_B^m \le x$. Unique factorization makes $F$ injective, since $v_q(F(f)) = f(q)$ for $q \le B$. The domain has $(m+1)^{\pi(B)}$ elements.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Scarcity]\label{thm:scarce}
For all $B, x$, $\Psi_B(x) \le (\lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor + 1)^{\pi(B)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Map a smooth $v \le x$ to its factor-base valuation vector. Each entry is at most $\lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor$ since $2^{v_p(v)} \le v \le x$. The map is injective on the smooth pool, since outside the factor base all valuations vanish.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Two-sided bracket]\label{cor:bracket}
If $P_B^{\,m} \le x$ then $(m+1)^{\pi(B)} \le \Psi_B(x) \le (\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1)^{\pi(B)}$. Hence for fixed $B$ the pool is polynomial in $\log x$ of degree exactly $\pi(B)$, so an additive shift of $\log x$ by $2\log p$ is a first-order effect on the count, matching Theorem \ref{thm:squeeze}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Abundance of the hit sub-pool]
Let $p \le B$ be prime. If $P_B^{\,m} \le \lfloor x/p^2\rfloor$ then $\hit_B(p^2;x) \ge (m+1)^{\pi(B)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Corollary \ref{cor:psq} followed by Theorem \ref{thm:abund} at the rescaled bound.
\end{proof}

\section{The $\FF_2$ blind spot}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sqmul}
For $a \ne 0$, $a^2 b$ is a perfect square iff $b$ is.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $b = c^2$ then $a^2b = (ac)^2$. Conversely if $a^2 b = d^2$ then $a^2 \mid d^2$, so $a \mid d$; write $d = ae$ and cancel $a^2 > 0$ to get $b = e^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$\FF_2$ blind spot]\label{thm:blindspot}
For any finite index set $S$, any $p > 0$, and any weights $w : S \to \NN$,
\[
\prod_{i \in S}(p^2 w_i) \text{ is a perfect square} \iff \prod_{i \in S} w_i \text{ is a perfect square}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\prod_{i\in S}(p^2w_i) = (p^{|S|})^2\prod_{i\in S}w_i$; apply Lemma \ref{lem:sqmul} with $a = p^{|S|} \ne 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Relations come from the cofactors]
Let $p > 0$ and $w_i > 0$ for $i$ in a finite index set $\iota$, with $p^2 w_i$ $B$-smooth for all $i$. If $|\iota| > \pi(B)$ then there is a nonempty $S \subseteq \iota$ with $\prod_{i\in S} w_i$ a perfect square.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The $\FF_2$ exponent vectors of the $|\iota| > \pi(B)$ smooth values $p^2 w_i$, in $\pi(B)$ factor-base coordinates, are linearly dependent, giving a nonempty $S$ with $\prod_{i\in S}p^2 w_i$ square. Theorem \ref{thm:blindspot} transfers the square to the cofactors.
\end{proof}

A $p^2$-hit contributes an even exponent to every member, hence the zero vector modulo $2$; it never changes the relation lattice. A prime-power hit spends smoothness budget without purchasing a new relation direction. This is why the prime-power feature \emph{predicts} yield rather than \emph{mimicking} it: it moves the budget without perturbing the $\FF_2$ combinatorics.

\section{The exactly solvable case $B = 2$}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:psi2}
For $x \ge 1$, $\Psi_2(x) = \lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
A positive integer is $2$-smooth iff it is a power of $2$; the powers $2^j \le x$ are those with $0 \le j \le \lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor$, and $j \mapsto 2^j$ is injective.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp budget law]
For $x \ge 4$, $\hit_2(4;x) + 2 = \Psi_2(x)$; equivalently the $4$-hit fraction is exactly $(u-1)/(u+1)$ with $u = \lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Corollary \ref{cor:psq} with $p=2$, $\hit_2(4;x) = \Psi_2(\lfloor x/4\rfloor)$, and $\lfloor x/4\rfloor \ge 1$. By Theorem \ref{thm:psi2} both sides are logarithms, and $\lfloor \log_2(x/4)\rfloor = \lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor - 2$ for $x \ge 4$.
\end{proof}

Hitting $4 = 2^2$ consumes exactly two units of the base-two budget --- the sharp instance of Theorem \ref{thm:squeeze}, with equality and no slack.

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Hit-count by rescaling}
To compute $\hit_B(m;x)$ for a $B$-smooth modulus $m$, compute $\Psi_B(\lfloor x/m\rfloor)$ rather than enumerating the hit set: a factor-$m$ saving in time and memory, compounding across all $(p,j)$ pairs when $\Psi_B$ is memoized. Correctness is Theorem \ref{thm:rescale}; the smoothness check on $m$ is mandatory by Remark \ref{rem:necessary}.

\subsection{Budget decomposition audit}
Theorem \ref{thm:decomp} gives a self-checking computation of the aggregate budget: compute $\sum_v \Omega(v)$ by direct factorization and independently $\sum_{p \le B}\sum_{j}\Psi_B(\lfloor x/p^j\rfloor)$ by repeated smooth counts. Agreement is guaranteed; disagreement localises a bug. The second route costs $O(\pi(B)\log x)$ smooth-count evaluations.

\subsection{Graded spectrum by telescoping}
Theorem \ref{thm:graded} computes the full multiplicity histogram of a factor-base prime from $\lfloor \log_p x\rfloor + 1$ smooth counts by successive differences, without factoring every pool element.

\subsection{Feature design}
The theory prescribes the feature set: $\one[p^j \mid v]$ for each factor-base prime $p$ and each layer $j$. Theorem \ref{thm:decomp} says these coordinates linearly span the budget; Theorem \ref{thm:complete} says they determine $v$; Theorem \ref{thm:blind} says truncating to $j = 1$ loses the budget entirely. The empirical configuration ($j = 2$, $p \le 13$) is the minimal nontrivial extension, and Theorem \ref{thm:antitone} predicts that its weight decays as $1/\log B$.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Why the failed features failed}
Mid-prime fractions and quadratic-residue density are global descriptors of the instance, not of the individual candidate's arithmetic; neither appears in any identity linking to $\Omega$ or $\Psi_B$. The prime-power indicators appear on the right-hand side of an exact linear identity for the budget (Theorem \ref{thm:decomp}). The empirical outcome is consonant with the structure, and the structure predicts it in advance.

\subsection{The graded picture}
The prime-power hit features are the graded coordinates of the multiplicative monoid of $B$-smooth integers, and the grading splits the information exactly in two. Layer $j = 1$ is the abelianization modulo squares: it carries precisely the $\FF_2$ relation data the sieve's linear algebra consumes, and by Theorem \ref{thm:blind} nothing about the budget. Layers $j \ge 2$ carry the budget --- by Theorem \ref{thm:decomp}, all of it --- and by Theorem \ref{thm:blindspot} nothing about the relation lattice. The two layers are information-theoretically disjoint by theorem, not merely weakly correlated in a sample. This is why the new features' contribution cannot be absorbed by re-weighting the baseline, and why it must generalise out of sample.

\subsection{Boundary conditions}
Two statements required guarding. First, $\hit_B(m;x) = \Psi_B(\lfloor x/m\rfloor)$ is false for non-smooth $m$ (Remark \ref{rem:necessary}); smoothness of the modulus is a hypothesis, not a convenience. Second, the real-valued bound of Theorem \ref{thm:squeeze} fails when $x < p^2$, where the floor collapses. Both are cases of ``true after the right definition''.

\section{Future work}

\begin{conjecture}[Hit fraction as a Dickman-type ratio]
For fixed $B$ and $x \to \infty$,
\[
\frac{\hit_B(p^2;x)}{\Psi_B(x)} = \frac{\Psi_B(\lfloor x/p^2\rfloor)}{\Psi_B(x)} \longrightarrow 1,
\]
with second-order rate $1 - \pi(B)\cdot\dfrac{2\log p}{\log x} + O\big((\log x)^{-2}\big)$; and for $B$ growing with $x$ in the tight-$u$ regime,
\[
\frac{\hit_B(p^2;x)}{\Psi_B(x)} = \frac{\rho\!\left(u - \frac{2\log p}{\log B}\right)}{\rho(u)} + o(1),
\]
where $\rho$ is the Dickman function and $u = \log x/\log B$.
\end{conjecture}

Theorem \ref{thm:rescale} converts every question about hit features into a question about $\Psi_B$ at two nearby arguments, so the entire predictive content of a hit feature is the local logarithmic derivative of $\Psi_B$. The fixed-$B$ leading term is consistent with Corollary \ref{cor:bracket}. The exact identity is settled; the missing ingredient is an asymptotic for $\Psi_B$, for which the fixed-$B$ case is elementary lattice-point counting that the bracket already half-provides.

Further directions: (i) determine the minimal sub-family of layers that remains a complete invariant on a pool bounded by $x$, giving a principled feature budget; (ii) extend Corollary \ref{cor:joint} to a full inclusion--exclusion for arbitrary squarefull moduli, converting the joint hit-feature distribution into a lattice of rescaled smooth counts and hence into a predictable correlation structure for the design matrix; (iii) study the $\FF_\ell$ analogue of Theorem \ref{thm:blindspot}, where layers $j \equiv 0 \pmod \ell$ become blind, giving a family of gradings interpolating between relation data and budget data.

\section{Conclusion}

Divisibility features on a smooth pool are not new arithmetic conditions; they are changes of the smoothness budget, exactly. From this single bijective observation follow a graded valuation spectrum, an exact $u$-shift of $2\log p/\log B$ antitone in $B$, a linear decomposition of the aggregate budget into prime-power hit counts, completeness of the prime-power profile as an invariant, provable blindness and forced collisions for its squarefree truncation, two-sided exponential abundance bounds, and the invisibility of prime-power hits to $\FF_2$ relation collection. Together these account, structurally and in advance, for the observed $+0.0892$ out-of-sample $R^2$ contributed by prime-power hit indicators, and for the failure of two plausible alternatives. The prime-power hit features are not a lucky covariate: they are the coordinate system in which the smoothness budget is linear.

  "demo": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Prime-power hits and the smoothness budget: numerical demonstrations.

Every theorem in the accompanying paper is an *exact* identity or inequality.
This script verifies each of them by brute force on concrete ranges, so the
reader can see the statements hold on the nose, with no error terms.

Contents
--------
 1. Exact rescaling:      hit_B(m; x) = Psi_B(floor(x/m))  for B-smooth m > 0
 2. Necessity of smoothness of the modulus (B=5, m=7, x=100: 0 != 10)
 3. Joint hits compose:   #{p^2|v and q^2|v} = Psi_B(x/(p^2 q^2))
 4. Graded spectrum:      #{v_p(v)=j} = Psi_B(x/p^j) - Psi_B(x/p^(j+1))
 5. Budget shift:         u(v) = u(v/p^2) + 2 log p / log B, and antitonicity
 6. Budget decomposition: sum_v Omega(v) = sum_p sum_j hit_B(p^j; x)
 7. Squarefree blindness and forced collisions
 8. Completeness of the prime-power profile
 9. Abundance bracket:    (m+1)^pi(B) <= Psi_B(x) <= (log2 x + 1)^pi(B)
10. F_2 blind spot:       prod p^2 w_i square  <=>  prod w_i square
11. Exactly solvable B=2: Psi_2(x) = log2(x)+1 and hit_2(4;x) + 2 = Psi_2(x)

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from collections import Counter
from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic arithmetic primitives (all inlined, no external dependencies)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def primes_upto(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes p with p <= n, by a simple sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i :: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i :: i]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def factorize(v: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Prime factorization of v >= 1 as {prime: exponent}."""
    assert v >= 1
    out: Dict[int, int] = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= v:
        while v % d == 0:
            out[d] = out.get(d, 0) + 1
            v //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if v > 1:
        out[v] = out.get(v, 0) + 1
    return out


def big_omega(v: int) -> int:
    """Omega(v): number of prime factors of v counted with multiplicity."""
    return sum(factorize(v).values())


def valuation(v: int, p: int) -> int:
    """The p-adic valuation v_p(v) for v >= 1."""
    assert v >= 1 and p >= 2
    e = 0
    while v % p == 0:
        v //= p
        e += 1
    return e


def is_smooth(B: int, v: int) -> bool:
    """v is B-smooth: every prime factor of v is at most B.  (v >= 1.)"""
    return all(p <= B for p in factorize(v))


def smooth_pool(B: int, x: int) -> List[int]:
    """All B-smooth v with 1 <= v <= x."""
    return [v for v in range(1, x + 1) if is_smooth(B, v)]


def psi(B: int, x: int) -> int:
    """Psi_B(x): the number of B-smooth integers in [1, x]."""
    if x < 1:
        return 0
    return len(smooth_pool(B, x))


def hit_count(B: int, m: int, x: int) -> int:
    """#{v <= x : v is B-smooth and m | v}."""
    return sum(1 for v in smooth_pool(B, x) if v % m == 0)


def primorial(B: int) -> int:
    """P_B = product of all primes <= B."""
    out = 1
    for p in primes_upto(B):
        out *= p
    return out


def sqf_hits(B: int, v: int) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Squarefree hit vector: the factor-base primes dividing v."""
    return tuple(p for p in primes_upto(B) if v % p == 0)


def pow_hits(B: int, v: int) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Prime-power hit vector: the factor-base primes p with p^2 | v."""
    return tuple(p for p in primes_upto(B) if v % (p * p) == 0)


def hit_profile(B: int, v: int, jmax: int) -> Tuple[Tuple[int, int], ...]:
    """The prime-power hit profile of v, truncated at layer jmax."""
    return tuple(
        (p, j)
        for p in primes_upto(B)
        for j in range(1, jmax + 1)
        if v % (p**j) == 0
    )


def is_perfect_square(n: int) -> bool:
    r = math.isqrt(n)
    return r * r == n


def u_param(B: int, x: int) -> float:
    """The smoothness parameter u = log x / log B."""
    return math.log(x) / math.log(B)


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 76)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Exact rescaling theorem
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_exact_rescaling() -> None:
    banner("1.  EXACT RESCALING:  hit_B(m; x) = Psi_B(floor(x/m))  for smooth m")
    print("A divisibility feature is not a new arithmetic condition on the pool;")
    print("it is a change of the smoothness budget.  The identity is exact.\n")
    print(f"{'B':>4} {'m':>6} {'x':>7} {'hit_B(m;x)':>12} {'Psi_B(x/m)':>12}  match")
    print("-" * 76)
    ok = True
    for B in (5, 7, 11, 13):
        for p in primes_upto(B):
            for j in (1, 2, 3):
                m = p**j
                for x in (500, 2000, 10000):
                    lhs = hit_count(B, m, x)
                    rhs = psi(B, x // m)
                    ok &= lhs == rhs
                    if (B, j, x) in {(5, 2, 2000), (13, 2, 10000), (7, 3, 2000)}:
                        print(
                            f"{B:>4} {m:>6} {x:>7} {lhs:>12} {rhs:>12}"
                            f"  {'OK' if lhs == rhs else 'FAIL'}"
                        )
    print(f"\nAll {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}: verified over B in {{5,7,11,13}},")
    print("all prime powers p^j (j<=3) with p <= B, and x in {500, 2000, 10000}.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Smoothness of the modulus is necessary
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_necessity() -> None:
    banner("2.  THE SMOOTHNESS HYPOTHESIS ON m IS NECESSARY")
    B, m, x = 5, 7, 100
    lhs = hit_count(B, m, x)
    rhs = psi(B, x // m)
    print(f"B = {B}, m = {m} (NOT {B}-smooth), x = {x}")
    print(f"  hit_B(m; x)          = {lhs}")
    print(f"  Psi_B(floor(x/m))    = {rhs}   <- 5-smooth numbers up to 14:")
    print(f"                              {smooth_pool(B, x // m)}")
    print(f"  Equal? {lhs == rhs}.  The failure is total, not an error term:")
    print("  the backward map w -> m*w leaves the smooth pool entirely.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Joint hits compose multiplicatively
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_joint_hits() -> None:
    banner("3.  JOINT HITS COMPOSE:  #{p^2|v, q^2|v} = Psi_B(x/(p^2 q^2))")
    print("Two prime-power features are NOT independent events; their joint")
    print("firing rate is the single-feature rate at the product modulus.\n")
    print(f"{'B':>4} {'p':>3} {'q':>3} {'x':>7} {'joint':>8} {'Psi_B(x/p2q2)':>15}  match")
    print("-" * 76)
    ok = True
    for B in (7, 13):
        for x in (5000, 50000):
            for p, q in combinations(primes_upto(B), 2):
                joint = sum(
                    1
                    for v in smooth_pool(B, x)
                    if v % (p * p) == 0 and v % (q * q) == 0
                )
                rhs = psi(B, x // (p * p * q * q))
                ok &= joint == rhs
                if (p, q) in {(2, 3), (3, 5)}:
                    print(
                        f"{B:>4} {p:>3} {q:>3} {x:>7} {joint:>8} {rhs:>15}"
                        f"  {'OK' if joint == rhs else 'FAIL'}"
                    )
    print(f"\nAll {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'} over all distinct pairs p,q <= B.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Graded valuation spectrum
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_graded_spectrum() -> None:
    banner("4.  GRADED SPECTRUM:  #{v_p(v)=j} = Psi_B(x/p^j) - Psi_B(x/p^(j+1))")
    B, x, p = 13, 20000, 3
    pool = smooth_pool(B, x)
    hist = Counter(valuation(v, p) for v in pool)
    print(f"B = {B}, x = {x}, p = {p}.   Pool size Psi_B(x) = {len(pool)}\n")
    print(f"{'j':>3} {'#(v_p = j)':>12} {'telescoped':>12}  match")
    print("-" * 76)
    ok = True
    total = 0
    for j in range(0, int(math.log(x, p)) + 2):
        direct = hist.get(j, 0)
        tele = psi(B, x // p**j) - psi(B, x // p ** (j + 1))
        ok &= direct == tele
        total += direct
        print(f"{j:>3} {direct:>12} {tele:>12}  {'OK' if direct == tele else 'FAIL'}")
    print(f"\nStrata sum to {total} = Psi_B(x) = {len(pool)}: {total == len(pool)}")
    print(f"All {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}.  The whole multiplicity histogram is a")
    print("telescoping family of rescaled smooth counts.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Budget shift and the tight-u mechanism
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_budget_shift() -> None:
    banner("5.  BUDGET SHIFT  u(v) = u(v/p^2) + 2 log p / log B,  ANTITONE IN B")
    print("Exact split (checked to machine precision):\n")
    print(f"{'B':>6} {'p':>3} {'v':>10} {'u(v)':>10} {'u(v/p^2)+toll':>15} {'err':>10}")
    print("-" * 76)
    worst = 0.0
    for B in (13, 1000):
        for p in (2, 3, 5):
            for w in (7, 11, 143):
                v = p * p * w
                lhs = u_param(B, v)
                toll = 2 * math.log(p) / math.log(B)
                rhs = u_param(B, v // (p * p)) + toll
                worst = max(worst, abs(lhs - rhs))
                if w == 143:
                    print(
                        f"{B:>6} {p:>3} {v:>10} {lhs:>10.6f} {rhs:>15.6f}"
                        f" {abs(lhs - rhs):>10.2e}"
                    )
    print(f"\nMaximum deviation over all cases: {worst:.3e}  (exact identity)\n")

    print("THE TIGHT-u MECHANISM.  The toll 2 log p / log B is ANTITONE in B:")
    print("the same prime-power hit eats a larger share of the budget at a")
    print("smaller factor base.  This is why the feature earns its weight at")
    print("small B (the experiment used p <= 13) and vanishes at large B.\n")
    print(f"{'B':>10}  " + "  ".join(f"toll(p={p}) " for p in (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13)))
    print("-" * 76)
    for B in (13, 50, 200, 1000, 10**4, 10**6):
        row = "  ".join(
            f"{2 * math.log(p) / math.log(B):>10.4f}" for p in (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13)
        )
        print(f"{B:>10}  {row}")
    print("\nAt B = 13 a 2^2-hit costs 0.54 units of u; at B = 10^6 it costs 0.10.")
    print("Since the smooth density rho(u) decays super-exponentially, half a")
    print("unit of u is a first-order effect in the tight-u regime.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Budget decomposition
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_budget_decomposition() -> None:
    banner("6.  BUDGET DECOMPOSITION:  sum_v Omega(v) = sum_p sum_j hit_B(p^j; x)")
    print("The prime-power hit counts are a LINEAR COORDINATE SYSTEM for the")
    print("total smoothness budget -- not a proxy for it.\n")
    print(f"{'B':>4} {'x':>7} {'sum Omega(v)':>14} {'sum of hits':>13} "
          f"{'rescaled form':>15}  match")
    print("-" * 76)
    ok = True
    for B in (5, 11, 13):
        for x in (1000, 8000, 30000):
            pool = smooth_pool(B, x)
            lhs = sum(big_omega(v) for v in pool)
            J = int(math.log2(x))
            mid = sum(
                hit_count(B, p**j, x)
                for p in primes_upto(B)
                for j in range(1, J + 1)
            )
            rhs = sum(
                psi(B, x // p**j)
                for p in primes_upto(B)
                for j in range(1, J + 1)
            )
            ok &= lhs == mid == rhs
            print(

                f"  {'OK' if lhs == mid == rhs else 'FAIL'}"

def demo_feature_information() -> None:

    for B, x in ((11, 20000), (13, 60000)):
        pool = smooth_pool(B, x)
        omegas = [big_omega(v) for v in pool]
        mean = sum(omegas) / len(omegas)
        tot_var = sum((o - mean) ** 2 for o in omegas) / len(omegas)

        def residual_variance(key) -> float:
            groups: Dict[object, List[int]] = {}
            for v in pool:
                groups.setdefault(key(v), []).append(big_omega(v))
            s = 0.0
            for vals in groups.values():
                mu = sum(vals) / len(vals)
                s += sum((o - mu) ** 2 for o in vals)
            return s / len(pool)

        r_sqf = residual_variance(lambda v: sqf_hits(B, v))
        r_pow = residual_variance(lambda v: (sqf_hits(B, v), pow_hits(B, v)))
        J = int(math.log2(x))
        r_full = residual_variance(lambda v: hit_profile(B, v, J))
        print(f"B = {B}, x = {x}, pool size {len(pool)}, Var[Omega] = {tot_var:.4f}")
        print(f"  conditioning on squarefree hits only:      "
              f"R^2 = {1 - r_sqf / tot_var:.4f}")
        print(f"  adding the prime-power (j=2) hits:         "
              f"R^2 = {1 - r_pow / tot_var:.4f}"
              f"   (gain {r_sqf / tot_var - r_pow / tot_var:+.4f})")
        print(f"  the full prime-power profile:              "
              f"R^2 = {1 - r_full / tot_var:.4f}   (complete invariant)\n")
    print("The gain from layer j=2 is structural: by the budget decomposition")
    print("the higher layers carry budget information that layer j=1 provably")
    print("cannot express.  This mirrors the measured out-of-sample increment")
    print("of +0.0892 R^2 (CI [0.041, 0.125]) from p^2-hit indicators (p <= 13),")

import math
from collections import Counter
from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic arithmetic primitives (all inlined, no external dependencies)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def primes_upto(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes p with p <= n, by a simple sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i :: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i :: i]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def factorize(v: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Prime factorization of v >= 1 as {prime: exponent}."""
    assert v >= 1
    out: Dict[int, int] = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= v:
        while v % d == 0:
            out[d] = out.get(d, 0) + 1
            v //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if v > 1:
        out[v] = out.get(v, 0) + 1
    return out


def big_omega(v: int) -> int:
    """Omega(v): number of prime factors of v counted with multiplicity."""
    return sum(factorize(v).values())


def valuation(v: int, p: int) -> int:
    """The p-adic valuation v_p(v) for v >= 1."""
    assert v >= 1 and p >= 2
    e = 0
    while v % p == 0:
        v //= p
        e += 1
    return e


def is_smooth(B: int, v: int) -> bool:
    """v is B-smooth: every prime factor of v is at most B.  (v >= 1.)"""
    return all(p <= B for p in factorize(v))


def smooth_pool(B: int, x: int) -> List[int]:
    """All B-smooth v with 1 <= v <= x."""
    return [v for v in range(1, x + 1) if is_smooth(B, v)]


def psi(B: int, x: int) -> int:
    """Psi_B(x): the number of B-smooth integers in [1, x]."""
    if x < 1:
        return 0
    return len(smooth_pool(B, x))


def hit_count(B: int, m: int, x: int) -> int:
    """#{v <= x : v is B-smooth and m | v}."""
    return sum(1 for v in smooth_pool(B, x) if v % m == 0)


def primorial(B: int) -> int:
    """P_B = product of all primes <= B."""
    out = 1
    for p in primes_upto(B):
        out *= p
    return out


def sqf_hits(B: int, v: int) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Squarefree hit vector: the factor-base primes dividing v."""
    return tuple(p for p in primes_upto(B) if v % p == 0)


def pow_hits(B: int, v: int) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Prime-power hit vector: the factor-base primes p with p^2 | v."""
    return tuple(p for p in primes_upto(B) if v % (p * p) == 0)


def hit_profile(B: int, v: int, jmax: int) -> Tuple[Tuple[int, int], ...]:
    """The prime-power hit profile of v, truncated at layer jmax."""
    return tuple(
        (p, j)
        for p in primes_upto(B)
        for j in range(1, jmax + 1)
        if v % (p**j) == 0
    )


def is_perfect_square(n: int) -> bool:
    r = math.isqrt(n)
    return r * r == n


def u_param(B: int, x: int) -> float:
    """The smoothness parameter u = log x / log B."""
    return math.log(x) / math.log(B)


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 76)

def demo_feature_information() -> None:
    banner("12.  WHY THE PRIME-POWER FEATURE ADDS SIGNAL: LAYER DISJOINTNESS")
    print("For each pool, we measure how much of the variation in the budget")
    print("Omega(v) survives after conditioning on the squarefree hit vector")
    print("(the baseline features) versus the prime-power hit vector.\n")
    for B, x in ((11, 20000), (13, 60000)):
        pool = smooth_pool(B, x)
        omegas = [big_omega(v) for v in pool]
        mean = sum(omegas) / len(omegas)
        tot_var = sum((o - mean) ** 2 for o in omegas) / len(omegas)

        def residual_variance(key) -> float:
            groups: Dict[object, List[int]] = {}
            for v in pool:
                groups.setdefault(key(v), []).append(big_omega(v))
            s = 0.0
            for vals in groups.values():
                mu = sum(vals) / len(vals)
                s += sum((o - mu) ** 2 for o in vals)
            return s / len(pool)

        r_sqf = residual_variance(lambda v: sqf_hits(B, v))
        r_pow = residual_variance(lambda v: (sqf_hits(B, v), pow_hits(B, v)))
        J = int(math.log2(x))
        r_full = residual_variance(lambda v: hit_profile(B, v, J))
        print(f"B = {B}, x = {x}, pool size {len(pool)}, Var[Omega] = {tot_var:.4f}")
        print(f"  conditioning on squarefree hits only:      "
              f"R^2 = {1 - r_sqf / tot_var:.4f}")
        print(f"  adding the prime-power (j=2) hits:         "
              f"R^2 = {1 - r_pow / tot_var:.4f}"
              f"   (gain {r_sqf / tot_var - r_pow / tot_var:+.4f})")
        print(f"  the full prime-power profile:              "
              f"R^2 = {1 - r_full / tot_var:.4f}   (complete invariant)\n")
    print("The gain from layer j=2 is structural: by the budget decomposition")
    print("the higher layers carry budget information that layer j=1 provably")
    print("cannot express.  This mirrors the measured out-of-sample increment")
    print("of +0.0892 R^2 (CI [0.041, 0.125]) from p^2-hit indicators (p <= 13),")

import math
from functools import lru_cache
from typing import List, Tuple


def primes_upto(n: int) -> List[int]:
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i :: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i :: i]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def smooth_pool(B: int, x: int) -> List[int]:
    if x < 1:
        return []
    pool: List[int] = [1]
    for p in primes_upto(B):
        nxt: List[int] = []
        for v in pool:
            w = v
            while w <= x:
                nxt.append(w)
                w *= p
        pool = nxt
    return sorted(pool)


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def psi(B: int, x: int) -> int:
    return len(smooth_pool(B, x))


def hit_fraction(B: int, p: int, x: int) -> float:
    """The exact p^2-hit fraction, via the rescaling identity."""
    return psi(B, x // (p * p)) / psi(B, x)


def first_order_prediction(B: int, p: int, x: int) -> float:
    """1 - pi(B) * 2 log p / log x."""
    return 1.0 - len(primes_upto(B)) * 2 * math.log(p) / math.log(x)


def power_law_prediction(B: int, p: int, x: int) -> float:
    """(1 - 2 log p / log x)^pi(B): the exact power-law surrogate."""
    k = len(primes_upto(B))
    base = 1.0 - 2 * math.log(p) / math.log(x)
    return base**k if base > 0 else 0.0


def toll(B: int, p: int) -> float:
    """The budget toll 2 log p / log B, in units of the smoothness parameter u."""
    return 2 * math.log(p) / math.log(B)

              f"{fo:>12.4f} {abs(f - pl):>10.4f}")

def psi(B: int, x: int) -> int:
    """Psi_B(x): the number of B-smooth integers in [1, x].  Memoized."""
    return len(smooth_pool(B, x))


def is_smooth(B: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """Test B-smoothness of m >= 1 by stripping factor-base primes."""
    if m < 1:
        return False
    for p in primes_upto(B):
        while m % p == 0:
            m //= p
    return m == 1


def hit_count_rescaled(B: int, m: int, x: int) -> int:
    """
    hit_B(m; x) via the exact rescaling identity.

    Raises ValueError if m is not a positive B-smooth modulus, because the
    identity genuinely fails there -- the guard is part of the algorithm.

    if m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("modulus must be positive")
    if not is_smooth(B, m):
        raise ValueError(
            f"modulus {m} is not {B}-smooth; the rescaling identity does not "
            f"apply (e.g. B=5, m=7, x=100 gives 0 != 10)"
        )
    return psi(B, x // m)

    """Reference implementation: enumerate the pool and filter.  Slow."""
    return sum(1 for v in smooth_pool(B, x) if v % m == 0)

    out: Dict[Tuple[int, int], int] = {}

            out[(p, j)] = hit_count_rescaled(B, m, x)
    return out

    """

    if p > B:
        raise ValueError(f"{p} is not in the factor base for B = {B}")

import math
from functools import lru_cache
from typing import Dict, List, NamedTuple, Tuple


def primes_upto(n: int) -> List[int]:

    pool: List[int] = [1]
    for p in primes_upto(B):

        for v in pool:

def valuation(v: int, p: int) -> int:
    e = 0
    while v % p == 0:
        v //= p
        e += 1
    return e


class BudgetAudit(NamedTuple):
    pool_size: int
    budget_direct: int          # sum_v Omega(v), by direct factorization
    budget_rescaled: int        # sum_{p,j} Psi_B(x / p^j)
    layers: Dict[int, int]      # j -> hits contributed at layer j
    cells: Dict[Tuple[int, int], int]   # (p, j) -> hit count
    agrees: bool


def budget_audit(B: int, x: int) -> BudgetAudit:
    """Compute the aggregate budget by both routes and attribute it to layers."""
    ps = primes_upto(B)
    pool = smooth_pool(B, x)

    # route 1: direct factorization of every pool element
    direct = sum(sum(valuation(v, p) for p in ps) for v in pool)

    # route 2: rescaled smooth counts, layer by layer
    J = max(1, int(math.log2(x))) if x >= 2 else 0
    cells: Dict[Tuple[int, int], int] = {}
    layers: Dict[int, int] = {}

        for p in ps:
            m = p**j
            if m > x:

            cells[(p, j)] = c

        budget_direct=direct,
        budget_rescaled=rescaled,
        layers=layers,
        cells=cells,
        agrees=direct == rescaled,

    tot = audit.budget_direct
    return {j: c / tot for j, c in audit.layers.items()} if tot else {}

           prime-power hit profiles tracks the pool size exactly (the profile is
           a complete invariant), while the number of distinct squarefree hit
           vectors saturates at the pigeonhole ceiling 2^pi(B).  The widening
           gap is the information the baseline features provably cannot see.

Requires: matplotlib, numpy.  Run:  python3 viz2.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from collections import Counter
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def primes_upto(n: int) -> List[int]:
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i :: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i :: i]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def smooth_pool(B: int, x: int) -> List[int]:
    pool = [1]
    for p in primes_upto(B):
        nxt: List[int] = []
        for v in pool:
            w = v
            while w <= x:
                nxt.append(w)
                w *= p
        pool = nxt
    return sorted(pool)


def psi(B: int, x: int) -> int:
    return 0 if x < 1 else len(smooth_pool(B, x))


def valuation(v: int, p: int) -> int:
    e = 0
    while v % p == 0:
        v //= p
        e += 1
    return e


def make_figure() -> None:
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15.5, 5.2))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 3, wspace=0.30)
    fig.suptitle(
        "A divisibility feature is an exact change of the smoothness budget",
        fontsize=14, fontweight="bold",
    )

    # ---------------- Panel A: rescaling scatter ----------------
    axA = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    xs, ys = [], []
    for B in (5, 7, 11, 13, 17):
        for x in (2000, 20000, 100000):
            pool = smooth_pool(B, x)
            for p in primes_upto(B):
                for j in range(1, 7):
                    m = p**j
                    if m > x:
                        continue
                    xs.append(sum(1 for v in pool if v % m == 0))
                    ys.append(psi(B, x // m))
    axA.scatter(xs, ys, s=16, alpha=0.55, color="#2563eb",
                label=f"smooth moduli ($n$ = {len(xs)})")
    top = max(xs + ys) * 1.06
    axA.plot([0, top], [0, top], color="#94a3b8", lw=1.2, ls="--", label="diagonal")
    # the deliberate counterexample: non-smooth modulus
    Bc, mc, xc = 5, 7, 100
    hc = sum(1 for v in smooth_pool(Bc, xc) if v % mc == 0)
    rc = psi(Bc, xc // mc)
    axA.scatter([hc], [rc], s=110, color="#dc2626", marker="X", zorder=5,
                label="non-smooth modulus\n($B$=5, $m$=7, $x$=100)")
    axA.set_xscale("symlog"); axA.set_yscale("symlog")
    axA.set_xlabel("observed hit count  $\\mathrm{hit}_B(p^j;x)$")
    axA.set_ylabel("predicted  $\\Psi_B(\\lfloor x/p^j\\rfloor)$")
    axA.set_title("A.  Exact rescaling: every smooth\nmodulus lands on the diagonal",
                  fontsize=10)
    axA.legend(fontsize=7.5, loc="upper left")
    axA.grid(alpha=0.25, ls=":")
    axA.set_axisbelow(True)

    # ---------------- Panel B: graded spectrum ----------------
    axB = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
    B, x, p = 13, 60000, 3
    pool = smooth_pool(B, x)
    hist = Counter(valuation(v, p) for v in pool)
    J = int(math.log(x, p)) + 1
    js = list(range(0, J + 1))
    observed = [hist.get(j, 0) for j in js]
    predicted = [psi(B, x // p**j) - psi(B, x // p ** (j + 1)) for j in js]
    w = 0.4
    axB.bar([j - w / 2 for j in js], observed, width=w, color="#0ea5e9",
            label="observed  $\\#\\{v_p(v)=j\\}$")
    axB.bar([j + w / 2 for j in js], predicted, width=w, color="#f59e0b",
            label="$\\Psi_B(x/p^{j}) - \\Psi_B(x/p^{j+1})$")
    axB.set_xticks(js)
    axB.set_xlabel(f"valuation  $v_{{{p}}}(v)$")
    axB.set_ylabel("number of pool members")
    axB.set_title(
        f"B.  Graded spectrum telescopes\n($B$ = {B}, $x$ = {x:,}, $p$ = {p};"
        f" max error {max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(observed, predicted))})",
        fontsize=10,
    )
    axB.legend(fontsize=8)
    axB.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25, ls=":")
    axB.set_axisbelow(True)

    # ---------------- Panel C: completeness vs blindness ----------------
    axC = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])
    B = 13
    ps = primes_upto(B)
    ceiling = 2 ** len(ps)
    Xs = [int(v) for v in np.unique(np.round(np.logspace(1, 5.4, 26)).astype(int))]
    pool_sizes, prof_counts, sqf_counts = [], [], []
    for x in Xs:
        pool = smooth_pool(B, x)
        pool_sizes.append(len(pool))
        prof_counts.append(len({
            tuple((q, valuation(v, q)) for q in ps) for v in pool
        }))
        sqf_counts.append(len({
            tuple(q for q in ps if v % q == 0) for v in pool
        }))
    axC.plot(Xs, pool_sizes, "o-", ms=3.5, color="#334155", lw=1.6,
             label="pool size  $\\Psi_B(x)$")
    axC.plot(Xs, prof_counts, "s--", ms=3.5, color="#0ea5e9", lw=1.6,
             label="distinct prime-power profiles")
    axC.plot(Xs, sqf_counts, "^-", ms=3.5, color="#dc2626", lw=1.6,
             label="distinct squarefree vectors")
    axC.axhline(ceiling, color="#dc2626", ls=":", lw=1.4)
    axC.text(Xs[1], ceiling * 1.15, f"pigeonhole ceiling  $2^{{\\pi(B)}}$ = {ceiling}",
             fontsize=8, color="#dc2626")
    axC.set_xscale("log"); axC.set_yscale("log")
    axC.set_xlabel("upper bound  $x$  (log scale)")
    axC.set_ylabel("count (log scale)")
    axC.set_title(
        f"C.  The profile is a complete invariant;\nits squarefree truncation saturates ($B$ = {B})",
        fontsize=10,
    )
    axC.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
    axC.grid(alpha=0.25, ls=":", which="both")
    axC.set_axisbelow(True)

    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.92))
    fig.savefig("rescaling_and_collapse.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote rescaling_and_collapse.png")
    print(f"panel A: {len(xs)} smooth moduli, "
          f"max |hit - Psi| = {max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(xs, ys))}")
    print(f"panel A counterexample: hit = {hc}, Psi = {rc}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    make_figure()

<script>
"use strict";

function primesUpto(n) {
  if (n < 2) return [];
  const s = new Uint8Array(n + 1).fill(1);
  s[0] = s[1] = 0;
  for (let i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) if (s[i]) for (let k = i * i; k <= n; k += i) s[k] = 0;
  const out = [];
  for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++) if (s[i]) out.push(i);
  return out;
}

// Generate the full B-smooth pool in [1, x] by closing {1} under multiplication
// by factor-base primes.  Far faster than trial-dividing every integer.
function smoothPool(B, x) {
  const ps = primesUpto(B);
  let pool = [1];
  for (const p of ps) {
    const next = [];
    for (const v of pool) {
      let w = v;
      while (w <= x) { next.push(w); w *= p; }
    }
    pool = next;
  }
  pool.sort((a, b) => a - b);
  return pool;
}

### Why repeated small primes tell you which numbers factor easily

---

## 0 · A number's secret budget

Pick a whole number and ask a deceptively simple question: is it built only out of **small** prime bricks?

$$1{,}048{,}575 \;=\; 3 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 11 \cdot 31 \cdot 41$$

The largest brick here is $41$. If "small" means "at most $50$", this number passes. If it means "at most $13$", it fails.

Numbers that pass have a name.

> **Definition.** A positive integer $v$ is **$B$-smooth** if every prime dividing $v$ is at most $B$. The threshold $B$ is the *factor-base bound*, and the primes $p \le B$ are the *factor base*. We write
> $$\Psi_B(x) \;=\; \#\{v : 1 \le v \le x,\ v \text{ is } B\text{-smooth}\}$$
> for the number of $B$-smooth values up to $x$, and $\pi(B)$ for the number of factor-base primes.

Smooth numbers are the hidden engine of modern integer factorization. Every serious factoring algorithm of the last forty years works the same way: generate a torrent of candidates, discard the ones that are not $B$-smooth, and assemble the survivors into a giant linear-algebra problem over the two-element field $\mathbb{F}_2$. The entire cost is governed by one number — **what fraction of your candidates survive the smoothness test?**

<details>
<summary><b>Background: why the survivors are useful at all</b> — click to expand</summary>

Once a candidate $v$ is known to be $B$-smooth, you know its complete factorization over the factor base, and hence its **exponent vector** $(v_p(v))_{p \le B}$. Reduce that vector modulo $2$. If you collect more than $\pi(B)$ such vectors they must be linearly dependent over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and a dependency is a sub-family whose product is a perfect square. In the classical sieves this yields a congruence of squares $a^2 \equiv b^2 \pmod N$, and $\gcd(a - b, N)$ is then a nontrivial factor of $N$ with constant probability. Everything hinges on producing smooth values fast enough — which is why predicting the yield matters. See the [Wikipedia article on smooth numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_number) and on the [quadratic sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_sieve) for the classical picture.

</details>

The yield is hard to predict in practice. Asymptotically the answer is elegant: setting the **smoothness parameter**

$$u \;=\; \frac{\log x}{\log B},$$

one has $\Psi_B(x) \approx x\,\rho(u)$ with $\rho$ the [Dickman function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function), which decays super-exponentially in $u$. But in the *tight-$u$ regime* where real sieves live — $u$ between roughly $2$ and $5$ — that asymptotic is a blunt instrument. What one wants is a per-instance dial.

---

## 1 · The empirical clue

A programme of experiments built exactly such a dial. The baseline model used the obvious features: candidate magnitude, the bound $B$, the derived $u$, and the **squarefree hit indicators** — for each factor-base prime $p$, does $p$ divide the candidate?

That baseline works well, but it leaves a residual. Two natural extra features failed to touch it:

| candidate feature | out-of-sample $R^2$ gain | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| mid-prime fraction of the factor base | $+0.019$ | confidence interval spans zero |
| quadratic-residue density | $+0.004$ | confidence interval spans zero |
| **prime-power hits: $p^2 \mid v$ for $p \le 13$** | $\mathbf{+0.0892}$ | **CI $[0.041,\,0.125]$ — decisive** |

*Repeated* small primes. Not which small primes divide your number, but which ones divide it **twice**.

The rest of this page explains why — and the explanation is not statistical. It is a chain of exact identities.

---

## 2 · The one idea: a divisibility test is a change of budget

Here is the theorem everything else follows from.

> **Exact Rescaling Theorem.** Let $m > 0$ be $B$-smooth. Then
> $$\#\{v \le x : v \text{ is } B\text{-smooth},\ m \mid v\} \;=\; \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/m\rfloor\big).$$

No error term. No asymptotic regime. An equality of integers.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof</b> — it is a two-line bijection</summary>

The map is $v \mapsto v/m$, with inverse $w \mapsto m\,w$.

*Forward.* If $1 \le v \le x$, $v$ is smooth, and $m \mid v$, then $v/m$ is an integer, at least $1$ (because $m \le v$) and at most $\lfloor x/m\rfloor$. It is smooth because **smoothness passes to divisors**: any prime of $v/m$ is a prime of $v$.

*Backward.* If $1 \le w \le \lfloor x/m\rfloor$ and $w$ is smooth, then $mw \le x$ by the defining property of floor division, and $mw$ is smooth because **smoothness is multiplicative** — the prime support of a product is the union of the supports — using here that $m$ itself is smooth.

The two maps are mutually inverse: $m \cdot (v/m) = v$ when $m \mid v$, and $(mw)/m = w$ since $m > 0$. $\blacksquare$

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Why the modulus <i>must</i> be smooth</b> — a total failure, not an error term</summary>

Take $B = 5$, $m = 7$, $x = 100$. No $5$-smooth number is divisible by $7$, so the left-hand side is $0$. But $\Psi_5(14) = |\{1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12\}| = 10$.

The backward map is what breaks: $7w$ leaves the smooth pool entirely. Smoothness of the modulus is a *hypothesis*, not a convenience — a detail worth savouring, because it is exactly the kind of side condition that a purely heuristic treatment would quietly drop.

</details>

**Read the theorem out loud.** Conditioning on $p^2 \mid v$ does not carve out some exotic subset of the pool. It reruns the *identical* smoothness question at a shrunken bound. A divisibility feature is a change of the smoothness budget.

Two immediate consequences. For distinct primes $p,q \le B$, joint hits compose multiplicatively,

$$\#\{v \le x : \text{smooth},\ p^2 \mid v,\ q^2 \mid v\} = \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/(p^2q^2)\rfloor\big),$$

and the *exact* multiplicity strata telescope,

$$\#\{v \le x : \text{smooth},\ v_p(v) = j\} \;=\; \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/p^j\rfloor\big) - \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/p^{j+1}\rfloor\big).$$

## 4 · The toll, and why it lives at small $B$

Translate the rescaling into the language of $u$. If $p^2 \mid v$ then, exactly,

$$u(v) \;=\; u(v/p^2) \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{2\log p}{\log B}}_{\text{the toll}}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Proof, and the boundary condition that bites</b></summary>

Write $v = p^2 w$. Then $v/p^2 = w$ exactly and $\log v = 2\log p + \log w$; divide by $\log B$.

The inequality form at the rescaled bound — $u(\lfloor x/p^2\rfloor) \le u(x) - 2\log p/\log B$ — needs the hypothesis $p^2 \le x$. If $x < p^2$ then $\lfloor x/p^2\rfloor = 0$ and the logarithm degenerates. Small print, but real: the guarded statement is the true one.

</details>

Now the observation that carries the whole empirical story:

> **Antitonicity of the toll.** For $1 < B \le B'$, $\ \dfrac{2\log p}{\log B'} \le \dfrac{2\log p}{\log B}.$

The *same* arithmetic event costs *more* budget at a *smaller* factor base. At $B = 10^6$, hitting $4$ costs $2\log 2/\log 10^6 \approx 0.10$ units of $u$ — a rounding error. At $B = 13$ it costs $\approx 0.54$ — over half a unit. And since $\rho$ decays super-exponentially, half a unit of $u$ is enormous.

That is why the effect is a *tight-$u$* phenomenon, and why the experiment found it with $p \le 13$.

## 5 · The theorem that makes it inevitable

Now the deepest result. The prime-power features do not merely add *some* budget information. They carry *all* of it, linearly.

Let $\Omega(v)$ count the prime factors of $v$ **with multiplicity** — the discrete smoothness budget.

> **Budget Decomposition Theorem.**
> $$\sum_{\substack{v \le x \\ \text{smooth}}} \Omega(v) \;=\; \sum_{p \le B}\;\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor} \#\{v \le x : \text{smooth},\ p^j \mid v\} \;=\; \sum_{p \le B}\;\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor} \Psi_B\big(\lfloor x/p^j\rfloor\big).$$

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof</b> — double counting, done cleanly</summary>

Two lemmas.

*The budget is a factor-base sum.* For a $B$-smooth $v$, $\ \Omega(v) = \sum_{p \le B} v_p(v)$, because primes outside the factor base contribute nothing.

*A valuation counts hits.* For $v \ne 0$ and prime $p$, $\ p^j \mid v \iff j \le v_p(v)$. So the number of layers $j \in [1,J]$ that fire is exactly $v_p(v)$, provided $J \ge v_p(v)$.

And $J = \lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor$ always suffices, because $2^{v_p(v)} \le p^{v_p(v)} \le v \le x$.

Combine: $\Omega(v) = \sum_{p\le B}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\mathbf{1}[p^j \mid v]$. Sum over the pool, exchange the two finite sums, and each $(p,j)$ term becomes a hit count. Apply the rescaling theorem to each modulus $p^j$ for the second equality. $\blacksquare$

</details>

**This is the whole story in one line.** The prime-power hit counts are a **linear coordinate system for the smoothness budget** — not a proxy that happens to correlate, but a basis in which the budget is literally a sum of coordinates. And the squarefree features are precisely the single layer $j = 1$ of a stack $\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor$ deep.

The algorithm below computes the budget by two logically independent routes and attributes it layer by layer. Run it and read off how much of the budget layer one carries.

## 6 · What the squarefree layer cannot see

The claim "layer one cannot see the budget" is not a soft statement about correlation. It is an impossibility theorem.

> **Blindness Theorem.** Let $p$ be a prime dividing $v \ne 0$ and let $k \ge 0$. Then $v$ and $v\cdot p^k$ have *identical* squarefree hit vectors, while
> $$\Omega(v \cdot p^k) = \Omega(v) + k.$$

Multiplying by a prime you already have changes nothing the squarefree features can detect, yet drives the budget up without bound. So the fibres of the squarefree feature map contain values of arbitrarily different budget: **no function of the squarefree hits recovers the budget.**

There is also a pigeonhole. There are only $2^{\pi(B)}$ possible squarefree vectors, so:

> **Collision Theorem.** If $2^{\pi(B)} < \Psi_B(x)$, then two *distinct* smooth values in $[1,x]$ share a squarefree hit vector.

At $B = 2$ this is unconditional and explicit: for $x \ge 4$ the values $2$ and $4$ already collide.

Contrast this with the full profile.

> **Complete Invariant Theorem.** Two positive $B$-smooth integers that trigger exactly the same prime-power hit features are equal.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof of completeness</b></summary>

By unique factorization it suffices to match every valuation. For a prime $p \le B$: since $p^{v_p(v)} \mid v$, the hypothesis gives $p^{v_p(v)} \mid w$, so $v_p(v) \le v_p(w)$; symmetrically $v_p(w) \le v_p(v)$. For a prime $p > B$: smoothness forces both valuations to vanish. $\blacksquare$

The prime-power profile is a perfect fingerprint of a smooth number. Its $j = 1$ truncation provably is not. That gap *is* the signal.

</details>

{{visualization:1}}

## 7 · The cost side: hits spend budget without buying relations

Why does the prime-power feature *predict* the sieve's yield rather than merely mimic it? Because of a complementary blindness — this time on the other side.

> **The $\mathbb{F}_2$ Blind Spot.** For any finite index set $S$, any $p > 0$, and any weights $w_i$,
> $$\prod_{i\in S}(p^2 w_i) \text{ is a perfect square} \iff \prod_{i\in S} w_i \text{ is a perfect square}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof and its consequence</b></summary>

Factor out: $\prod_{i\in S}(p^2 w_i) = (p^{|S|})^2 \prod_{i\in S} w_i$, and multiplying by a nonzero square never changes squareness. (If $a^2 b = d^2$ then $a^2 \mid d^2$, so $a \mid d$; write $d = ae$ and cancel.) $\blacksquare$

**Consequence.** Given more than $\pi(B)$ smooth $p^2$-hits, some nonempty sub-family has a perfect-square product — and by the theorem that same relation is already present, unchanged, among the rescaled *cofactors*. The doubled prime contributes an even exponent to every member and so vanishes modulo $2$.

</details>

**A prime-power hit spends smoothness budget without buying a new relation direction.** Pure cost, no benefit — which is precisely what makes it a clean, exogenous predictor of yield: it moves the budget without perturbing the relation combinatorics.

---

## 8 · Is the hit sub-pool big enough to matter?

Yes, and by exact combinatorics rather than estimate. Let $P_B = \prod_{p\le B} p$.

> **Abundance bracket.** If $P_B^{\,m} \le x$ then
> $$(m+1)^{\pi(B)} \;\le\; \Psi_B(x) \;\le\; \big(\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor + 1\big)^{\pi(B)}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal both bounds</b></summary>

*Lower.* Every exponent vector $f : \{p \le B\} \to \{0,\dots,m\}$ gives a distinct smooth value $\prod p^{f(p)} \le P_B^m \le x$. Unique factorization makes the assignment injective, and there are $(m+1)^{\pi(B)}$ vectors.

*Upper.* Map a smooth $v \le x$ to its valuation vector. Each entry is at most $\lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor$ since $2^{v_p(v)} \le v \le x$, and the map is injective on the smooth pool.

</details>

So the pool is **polynomial in $\log x$ of degree exactly $\pi(B)$**. Applying the lower bound at the rescaled bound $x/p^2$ shows the $p^2$-hit sub-pool is itself exponentially large in $\pi(B)$. And because the exponent is $\pi(B)$, shifting $\log x$ by $2\log p$ is a *first-order* effect on the count — which is the counting-side shadow of the budget toll.

At $B = 2$ everything is closed-form: $\Psi_2(x) = \lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor + 1$, and for $x \ge 4$,
$$\#\{v \le x : 4 \mid v,\ v \text{ a power of }2\} + 2 = \Psi_2(x).$$
Hitting $4$ consumes exactly two units of the base-two budget. Equality, no slack.

## 11 · The picture that emerges

Step back and a single statement organises everything.

> The prime-power hit features are the **graded coordinates of the multiplicative monoid of smooth numbers**, and the grading splits the information exactly in two:
>
> - **Layer $j = 1$** — squarefree hits — is the abelianization modulo squares. It sees the $\mathbb{F}_2$ relation data a sieve consumes, and *nothing else*.
> - **Layers $j \ge 2$** see the smoothness budget, and *nothing else*.

These two kinds of information are **disjoint by theorem**, not merely weakly correlated in a sample. That is why adding "$p^2$ divides $v$" to a squarefree-hit baseline produces genuine out-of-sample gain: the new coordinates span a direction the old ones provably cannot reach, so the contribution cannot be absorbed by re-weighting, and it must generalise. And it is why the gain concentrates at small $B$: the toll the new features measure is antitone in $B$.

There is a moral here about model-building. Two plausible features failed; one succeeded. In hindsight the difference is structural rather than statistical — the successful feature has an exact identity behind it, an identity saying it reconstructs the very quantity the yield depends on. When a feature works, ask not only *how much* it explains but *what theorem it is a shadow of*.

<details>
<summary><b>Where this goes next</b> — the open conjecture</summary>

Because the rescaling identity converts every question about hit features into a question about $\Psi_B$ at two nearby arguments, the natural conjecture is sharp: for fixed $B$ and $x \to \infty$,
$$\frac{\Psi_B(x/p^2)}{\Psi_B(x)} \;=\; 1 - \pi(B)\cdot\frac{2\log p}{\log x} + O\big((\log x)^{-2}\big),$$

$$\frac{\Psi_B(x/p^2)}{\Psi_B(x)} \;=\; \frac{\rho\!\left(u - \frac{2\log p}{\log B}\right)}{\rho(u)} + o(1).$$
The exact identity is settled. What remains is an asymptotic for $\Psi_B$ itself — and for fixed $B$ that is elementary lattice-point counting, which the abundance bracket already half-provides.

Further questions: what is the *minimal* set of layers that remains a complete invariant on a pool bounded by $x$ (a principled feature budget rather than a heuristic cutoff)? Does the joint-hit composition extend to a full inclusion–exclusion over squarefull moduli, giving an analytically predictable correlation structure for the design matrix? And what does a relation stage modulo $\ell$-th powers see — there the layers $j \equiv 0 \pmod \ell$ go blind, suggesting a whole family of gradings interpolating between relation data and budget data?

</details>

pool, the total budget `∑ Ω(v)` equals the sum of the prime-power hit counts
`∑_{p ≤ B} ∑_{j ≥ 1} hit(p^j)`.  Via cycle one's rescaling this is
`∑_{p ≤ B} ∑_{j ≥ 1} Ψ_B(x / p^j)` (`sum_bigOmega_eq_sum_smoothCount`): the
prime-power features are a *linear coordinate system* for the budget, which the
squarefree features (only the `j = 1` layer) are not.

**Q2 (are the hit features a complete invariant?).**  Yes.
`smooth_eq_of_hitProfile_eq`: two positive `B`-smooth values with the same
prime-power hit profile are equal.  So the feature family is *complete*, while
`exists_sqfHits_collision` shows its `j = 1` truncation provably collides as
soon as the pool outgrows `2 ^ π(B)` — an unavoidable pigeonhole, made
unconditional at `B = 2` in `exists_sqfHits_collision_two`.

## Main results

* `bigOmega_eq_sum_primesBelow` — the budget of a smooth value is the sum of its
  factor-base valuations.
* `factorization_eq_card_filter` — a valuation is the number of prime-power hits
  it triggers.
* `sum_bigOmega_eq_sum_hitCount`, `sum_bigOmega_eq_sum_smoothCount` — **the
  budget decomposition**.
* `smooth_eq_of_hitProfile_eq` — the prime-power profile is a complete invariant
  of a smooth value.
* `exists_sqfHits_collision`, `exists_sqfHits_collision_two` — the squarefree
  truncation is provably incomplete.
-/

namespace PrimePowerBudget

open Finset

/-! ## The budget as a sum of valuations -/

lemma bigOmega_eq_sum_primeFactors (v : ℕ) :
    bigOmega v = ∑ p ∈ v.primeFactors, v.factorization p := by
  have := ArithmeticFunction.cardFactors_eq_sum_factorization (n := v)
  rw [ArithmeticFunction.cardFactors_apply] at this
  simpa [bigOmega, Finsupp.sum, Nat.support_factorization] using this

/-- For a `B`-smooth value the budget is the sum of its factor-base valuations:
primes outside the factor base contribute nothing. -/
lemma bigOmega_eq_sum_primesBelow {B v : ℕ} (hsm : Sm B v) :
    bigOmega v = ∑ p ∈ Nat.primesBelow (B + 1), v.factorization p := by
  rw [bigOmega_eq_sum_primeFactors]
  refine Finset.sum_subset ?_ ?_
  · intro p hp
    exact Nat.mem_primesBelow.2 ⟨by have := hsm p hp; omega, Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hp⟩
  · intro p _ hnot
    rw [← Nat.support_factorization] at hnot
    simpa using Finsupp.notMem_support_iff.1 hnot

/-- Every valuation of `v` is bounded by `log₂ v`: the base-two budget bounds all
prime-power exponents. -/
lemma factorization_le_log_two {p v : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hv : v ≠ 0) :
    v.factorization p ≤ Nat.log 2 v := by
  have h1 : p ^ (v.factorization p) ∣ v := Nat.ordProj_dvd v p
  have h2 : (2 : ℕ) ^ (v.factorization p) ≤ p ^ (v.factorization p) :=
    Nat.pow_le_pow_left hp.two_le _
  have h3 : p ^ (v.factorization p) ≤ v := Nat.le_of_dvd (Nat.pos_of_ne_zero hv) h1
  exact (Nat.le_log_iff_pow_le (by norm_num) hv).2 (le_trans h2 h3)

/-- **A valuation counts prime-power hits.**  As long as the window `[1, J]`
reaches the valuation, `v_p(v)` is exactly the number of exponents `j` for which
the hit feature `p ^ j ∣ v` fires. -/
lemma factorization_eq_card_filter {p v J : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hv : v ≠ 0)
    (hJ : v.factorization p ≤ J) :
    v.factorization p = ((Finset.Icc 1 J).filter (fun j => p ^ j ∣ v)).card := by
  have hset : ((Finset.Icc 1 J).filter (fun j => p ^ j ∣ v))
      = Finset.Icc 1 (v.factorization p) := by
    ext j
    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_Icc]
    rw [Nat.Prime.pow_dvd_iff_le_factorization hp hv]
    omega
  rw [hset, Nat.card_Icc]
  omega

/-! ## The budget decomposition -/

/-- **Budget decomposition (hit form).**  Summed over the whole `B`-smooth pool
below `x`, the smoothness budget is exactly the total number of prime-power hits:
`∑_v Ω(v) = ∑_{p ≤ B} ∑_{j = 1}^{⌊log₂ x⌋} hit(p^j)`.

This is the precise sense in which the prime-power features *carry* the budget:
they are not a heuristic proxy for it, they are a linear coordinate system for
it.  The squarefree features are the single layer `j = 1` of this sum. -/
theorem sum_bigOmega_eq_sum_hitCount (B x : ℕ) :
    ∑ v ∈ (Finset.Icc 1 x).filter (fun v => Sm B v), bigOmega v
      = ∑ p ∈ Nat.primesBelow (B + 1), ∑ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Nat.log 2 x),
          hitCount B (p ^ j) x := by
  classical
  set J := Nat.log 2 x with hJ
  set P := (Finset.Icc 1 x).filter (fun v => Sm B v) with hP
  have hstep : ∀ v ∈ P, bigOmega v
      = ∑ p ∈ Nat.primesBelow (B + 1), ∑ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 J,
          (if p ^ j ∣ v then 1 else 0) := by
    intro v hv
    simp only [hP, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_Icc] at hv
    obtain ⟨⟨hv1, hvx⟩, hsm⟩ := hv
    have hv0 : v ≠ 0 := by omega
    rw [bigOmega_eq_sum_primesBelow hsm]
    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    intro p hp
    have hpp := Nat.prime_of_mem_primesBelow hp
    have hle : v.factorization p ≤ J :=
      le_trans (factorization_le_log_two hpp hv0) (Nat.log_mono_right hvx)
    rw [factorization_eq_card_filter hpp hv0 hle, Finset.card_filter]
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl hstep, Finset.sum_comm]
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
  intro p hp
  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
  intro j _
  rw [← Finset.card_filter]
  unfold hitCount
  congr 1
  rw [hP, Finset.filter_filter]

/-- **Budget decomposition (rescaled form).**  Combining with cycle one's exact
rescaling, the total budget of the smooth pool is a sum of smooth counts at
geometrically rescaled bounds. -/
theorem sum_bigOmega_eq_sum_smoothCount (B x : ℕ) :
    ∑ v ∈ (Finset.Icc 1 x).filter (fun v => Sm B v), bigOmega v
      = ∑ p ∈ Nat.primesBelow (B + 1), ∑ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Nat.log 2 x),
          smoothCount B (x / p ^ j) := by
  rw [sum_bigOmega_eq_sum_hitCount]
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
  intro p hp
  have hpp := Nat.prime_of_mem_primesBelow hp
  have hpB : p ≤ B := by have := Nat.lt_of_mem_primesBelow hp; omega
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
  intro j _
  refine hitCount_eq_smoothCount B (p ^ j) x (pow_pos hpp.pos j) ?_
  intro q hq
  have hqp := Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hq
  have : q = p := (Nat.prime_dvd_prime_iff_eq hqp hpp).1
    (hqp.dvd_of_dvd_pow (Nat.dvd_of_mem_primeFactors hq))
  omega

/-! ## Completeness of the prime-power profile -/

/-- **The prime-power hit profile is a complete invariant.**  Two positive
`B`-smooth values that trigger exactly the same prime-power hit features are
equal.  Contrast `squarefree_features_blind`: the `j = 1` truncation of this
profile has infinite fibres. -/
theorem smooth_eq_of_hitProfile_eq {B v w : ℕ} (hv : 0 < v) (hw : 0 < w)
    (hsv : Sm B v) (hsw : Sm B w)
    (h : ∀ p ≤ B, ∀ j : ℕ, (p ^ j ∣ v ↔ p ^ j ∣ w)) : v = w := by
  refine Nat.eq_of_factorization_eq hv.ne' hw.ne' ?_
  intro p
  by_cases hp : p.Prime
  · by_cases hpB : p ≤ B
    · have h1 : v.factorization p ≤ w.factorization p := by
        rw [← Nat.Prime.pow_dvd_iff_le_factorization hp hw.ne']
        exact (h p hpB (v.factorization p)).1 (Nat.ordProj_dvd v p)
      have h2 : w.factorization p ≤ v.factorization p := by
        rw [← Nat.Prime.pow_dvd_iff_le_factorization hp hv.ne']
        exact (h p hpB (w.factorization p)).2 (Nat.ordProj_dvd w p)

    · have hv0 : v.factorization p = 0 := by
        by_contra hne
        exact hpB (hsv p (Nat.mem_primeFactors.2 ⟨hp,

      have hw0 : w.factorization p = 0 := by
        by_contra hne
        exact hpB (hsw p (Nat.mem_primeFactors.2 ⟨hp,
          Nat.dvd_of_factorization_pos hne, hw.ne'⟩))
      rw [hv0, hw0]
  · rw [Nat.factorization_eq_zero_of_not_prime _ hp,
      Nat.factorization_eq_zero_of_not_prime _ hp]

/-- **The squarefree truncation must collide.**  Once the smooth pool is larger

    Finset.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt_of_maps_to hcard hmaps
  exact ⟨v, hv, w, hw, hne, heq⟩

theorem exists_sqfHits_collision_two {x : ℕ} (hx : 4 ≤ x) :

  have hcount : smoothCount 2 x = Nat.log 2 x + 1 := smoothCount_two (by omega)

  rw [show (2 : ℕ) + 1 = 3 from rfl, hpi, hcount]
  omega
